newsitem.title: USA: Russia committed to space station work - official.
newsitem.headline: Russia committed to space station work - official.

text.p: Facing U.S. doubts about Russia's financial commitment to the international space station, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told Vice President Al Gore, "I'm going to make sure it gets done," a U.S. senior official said on Saturday.

"There was a very plain 'What do we have to do, how to we have to do it' discussion involving the vice president and the prime minister ...," the official said. "They laid it out and the prime minister said, 'I'm going to make sure it gets done.'"

In forthright talks on Thursday and Friday along with the heads of the U.S. and Russian space agencies, Chernomyrdin and Gore discussed concerns that financial problems in Russia could further delay and perhaps jeopardise the $40 billion space station project.

"The prime minister understood exactly what he was hearing, and said 'We can do this. And we will do this,'" the official told reporters travelling with Gore to Chicago, where the two dignitaries attended an auto show and courted U.S. investment in Russia.
The official voiced confidence that Russia's contribution to the space station would go forward, notably because of the "tremendous national pride" Russians had invested in their space programme.

"The space programme is one of the great clusters of Russian excellence ... which is still virtually intact coming out of the collapse of the Soviet Union. This is the place where many of their brightest people are spending their careers," the official said.

Russia's ability to pay for its part of the space station has been called into question on Capitol Hill, where Representative James Sensenbrenner, a Wisconsin Democrat, has suggested that Moscow withdraw as a full partner in the project.

Other partners in the venture include the space agencies of the United States, Europe, Canada and Japan. Many have already constructed their modules for the station, which is being designed to conduct experiments in the near-weightless environment of the Earth's orbit.
Russia is several months behind schedule on delivering a key component of the station, the module where the crew will live during the actual construction of the project.
